Transformers are Inherently Succinct

Pascal Bergsträßer Affiliation: RPTU Kaiserslautern-Landau Affiliation: Kaiserslautern, Germany Email: bergstraesser@cs.uni-kl.de    Ryan Cotterell Affiliation: ETH Zürich Affiliation: Zürich, Switzerland Email: ryan.cotterell@inf.ethz.ch    Anthony W. Lin Affiliation: RPTU Kaiserslautern-Landau and MPI-SWS Affiliation: Kaiserslautern, Germany Email: lin@cs.uni-kl.de
Abstract

We propose succinctness as a measure of the expressive power of a transformer in describing a concept. To this end, we prove that transformers are highly expressive in that they can represent formal languages substantially more succinctly than standard representations of formal languages like finite automata and Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) formulas. As a by-product of this expressivity, we show that verifying properties of transformers is provably intractable (i.e. EXPSPACE-complete).

1 Introduction

Transformers (Vaswani et al., 2017) are the underlying model behind the recent success of Large Language Models (LLMs). The past few years saw a large amount of theoretical development explaining the expressive power of transformers (Strobl et al., 2024; Barceló et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024; Hahn, 2020; Pérez et al., 2021; Chiang & Cholak, 2022; Jerad et al., 2025), their trainability and length generalizability (Zhou et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025; Chiang & Cholak, 2022), and the extent to which one can formally verify them (Sälzer et al., 2025). Interestingly, it is known that transformers with fixed (finite) precision (Yang et al., 2024; Barceló et al., 2024; Jerad et al., 2025; Li & Cotterell, 2025) recognize a well-known subclass of regular languages called star-free languages. Fixed-precision transformers are especially pertinent to real-world transformers, which are implemented on hardware with fixed (finite) precision.

Star-free languages form a rather small subclass of regular languages. More precisely, a star-free regular expression allows the intersection and complementation operators instead of the Kleene star. For this reason, the regular language a∗​b∗a^{*}b^{*} is star-free because it can be defined as ∅¯.b.a.∅¯¯\overline{\bar{\emptyset}.b.a.\bar{\emptyset}}. On the other hand, it is known that regular languages like (a​a)∗(aa)^{*} are not star-free (cf. see (Straubing, 1994)). This is in contrast to Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN), which can recognize all regular languages (Siegelmann & Sontag, 1995; Merrill et al., 2020). Thus, expressivity as language recognizers per se is perhaps not the most useful criterion for an LLM architecture.

In this paper, we propose succinctness as an alternative angle in understanding the “expressivity” of transformers. More precisely, the succinctness of a language LL with respect to a class 𝒞\mathcal{C} of language recognizers (e.g. transformers, automata, etc.) measures the smallest (denotational) size of T∈𝒞T\in\mathcal{C} that recognizes LL, i.e., how many symbols are used to describe TT. Succinctness has been studied in logic in computer science (e.g. (Grohe & Schweikardt, 2004; Stockmeyer, 1974)) as an alternative (and more computational) measure of expressiveness, and has direct consequence in how computationally difficult it is to analyze a certain expression. For example, Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) (Pnueli, 1977) is expressively equivalent to star-free regular languages (e.g. see (Libkin, 2004)), as well as a subclass of deterministic finite automata called counter-free automata (McNaughton & Papert, 1971). Despite this, it is known that LTL can be exponentially more succinct than finite automata (Sistla & Clarke, 1985). In other words, certain concepts can be described considerably more succinctly by LTL formulas as by finite automata. This has various consequences, e.g., analyzing LTL formulas (e.g. checking whether they describe a trivial concept) is provably computationally more difficult than analyzing finite automata (Sistla & Clarke, 1985).

Contributions.

Our main result can be summarized as follows:

Transformers can describe concepts extremely succinctly.

More precisely, we show that transformers are exponentially more succinct than LTL and RNN (so including state-of-the-art State-Space Models (SSMs), e.g., see (Gu & Dao, 2023; Merrill et al., 2024)), and doubly exponentially more succinct than finite automata. This means that, with the same descriptional size, transformers can encode complex patterns that require exponentially (resp. doubly exponentially) larger descriptional sizes for LTL and RNN (resp. automata). As a by-product of this expressivity, one may surmise that analyzing transformers must be computationally challenging. We show this to be the case. That is, verifying simple properties about transformers (e.g. whether it recognizes a trivial language) is computationally difficult: 𝖤𝖷𝖯𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤{\mathsf{EXPSPACE}}-complete. That is, with standard complexity-theoretic assumptions, this cannot be done in better than double exponential time.

In fact, we also show matching upper bound on the succinctness gap for LTL (exponential) and automata (double exponential). That is, we provide a translation from fixed-precision transformers to exponential-sized LTL formulas. This significantly improves the previously shown doubly exponential translation by Yang et al. (2024). As a consequence, for any fixed-precision transformer, there is an LTL formula (resp. finite automaton) of (doubly) exponential size recognizing the same language.

In proving our succinctness results, we show how transformers can count from 0 up to 22n2^{2^{n}}, i.e., the so-called “(doubly exponentially) large counters”. This requires a subtle encoding of large counters using attention. We then prove that the resulting languages using LTL and RNN (resp. finite automata) require exponentially (resp. doubly exponentially) larger description.

What assumptions do we use in our results? We assume that transformers and RNN are of a fixed (finite) precision. This assumption is faithful to real-world implementations, which use only fixed-precision arithmetics. We also use Unique-Hard Attention Transformers (UHAT), which are known to be expressively the weakest class of transformers (Hao et al., 2022), e.g., their languages are known to be in a very low complexity class AC0\text{AC}^{0}, whereas other classes of transformers (e.g. average-hard attention or softmax) can recognize languages beyond AC0\text{AC}^{0} (e.g. majority). Additionally, UHATs have also been used as transformer models in theoretical works of transformers (cf. (Yang et al., 2024; Jerad et al., 2025; Strobl et al., 2024; Hao et al., 2022; Li & Cotterell, 2025; Hahn, 2020; Barceló et al., 2024; Bergsträßer et al., 2024)).

Organization.

We recall some formal concepts (transformers, automata, and logic) in Section 2. We show in Section 3 how transformers can encode an exponential tiling problem. We show in Section 4 how this implies succinctness of UHATs relative to other representations. Applications of our results for reasoning about transformers are discussed in Section 5. We conclude the paper in Section 6.

2 Preliminaries

We often denote vectors by boldface letters and for a vector 𝒗=(v1,…,vd)\bm{v}=(v_{1},\dots,v_{d}) we write 𝒗⁡[i,j]:=(vi,…,vj)\bm{v}[i,j]:=(v_{i},\dots,v_{j}) for all 1≤i≤j≤d1\leq i\leq j\leq d and if i=ji=j, we simply write 𝒗⁡(i)\bm{v}(i). We also write 𝒏\bm{n} for a number nn to denote a vector (n,…,n)(n,\dots,n) of appropriate dimension.

An alphabet is a finite set Σ\Sigma of symbols (a.k.a. tokens). We write Σ∗\Sigma^{*} for the set of all words (a.k.a. sequences, strings) of the form a1​…​ana_{1}\dots a_{n}, where n≥0n\geq 0 and ai∈Σa_{i}\in\Sigma for all i∈[1,n]i\in[1,n]. A language is a subset L⊆Σ∗L\subseteq\Sigma^{*}. We assume familiarity with basic concepts in formal language theory and complexity theory (see e.g. (Kozen, 1997; Sipser, 1997)). In particular, we will deal with finite automata. We will also use the following complexity classes:

𝖯⊆𝖭𝖯⊆𝖯𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤⊆𝖤𝖷𝖯⊆𝖭𝖤𝖷𝖯⊆𝖤𝖷𝖯𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤.{\mathsf{P}}\subseteq{\mathsf{NP}}\subseteq{\mathsf{PSPACE}}\subseteq{\mathsf{EXP}}\subseteq{\mathsf{NEXP}}\subseteq{\mathsf{EXPSPACE}}.

The complexity classes 𝖯{\mathsf{P}} and 𝖭𝖯{\mathsf{NP}} correspond to problems solvable in polynomial (resp. nondeterminsitic polynomial) time, and are well-known. The complexity classes 𝖤𝖷𝖯{\mathsf{EXP}} and 𝖭𝖤𝖷𝖯{\mathsf{NEXP}} are similar to 𝖯{\mathsf{P}} and 𝖭𝖯{\mathsf{NP}}, but we allow the algorithm to use exponential time. The complexity classes 𝖯𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤{\mathsf{PSPACE}} and 𝖤𝖷𝖯𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤{\mathsf{EXPSPACE}} correspond to problems solvable in polynomial (resp. exponential) space. The above inclusions are well-known (cf. (Sipser, 1997)).

w,i⊧φ1∧φ2w,i\models\varphi_{1}\wedge\varphi_{2} iff w,i⊧φ1w,i\models\varphi_{1} and w,i⊧φ2w,i\models\varphi_{2}

w,i⊧φ1Uφ2w,i\models\varphi_{1}\mathbin{\textbf{U}}\varphi_{2} iff for some jj with i<j≤ni<j\leq n we have w,j⊧φ2w,j\models\varphi_{2} and
for all kk with i<k<ji<k<j we have w,k⊧φ1w,k\models\varphi_{1}

Moreover, we define the shortcuts

Pφ:=⊤SφFφ:=⊤UφXφ:=⊥UφGφ:=φ∧¬F¬φ.\textbf{P}\varphi:=\top\mathbin{\textbf{S}}\varphi\qquad\textbf{F}\varphi:=\top\mathbin{\textbf{U}}\varphi\qquad\textbf{X}\varphi:=\bot\mathbin{\textbf{U}}\varphi\qquad\textbf{G}\varphi:=\varphi\wedge\neg\textbf{F}\neg\varphi.

Example 1.

The star-free language (a​b)∗(ab)^{*} can be defined in LTL as

G​(Qa→X​Qb)∧G​(Qb∧X⊤→X​Qa).\textbf{G}(Q_{a}\to\textbf{X}Q_{b})\wedge\textbf{G}(Q_{b}\wedge\textbf{X}\top\to\textbf{X}Q_{a}).

In words, at any aa-position, the next letter is bb. At any bb-position that has a successor, the next letter is aa.

2.2 Masked unique hard-attention transformers

Let Σ\Sigma be a finite alphabet of tokens. A token embedding is a function 𝑒𝑚𝑏:Σ→ℚd\mathit{emb}\colon\Sigma\to\mathbb{Q}^{d} for some d>0d>0. A token embedding naturally extends to a homomorphism Σ∗→(ℚd)∗\Sigma^{*}\to(\mathbb{Q}^{d})^{*}, where 𝑒𝑚𝑏⁡(a1​…​an)=𝑒𝑚𝑏⁡(a1)​…​𝑒𝑚𝑏​(an)\mathit{emb}(a_{1}\dots a_{n})=\mathit{emb}(a_{1})\dots\mathit{emb}(a_{n}) for a1,…,an∈Σa_{1},\dots,a_{n}\in\Sigma.

Remark 2.

In the following we define transformers over arbitrary rational numbers since our upper bounds even hold in this setting. We remark that all of our results also hold for the special case of fixed-precision real numbers, i.e., with a constant number of bits for a fixed transformer regardless of the input length. In fact, the lower bounds already hold for integers of fixed precision.

Attention layer.

A masked unique hard-attention (UHA) layer of width r>0r>0 is defined by

  • •

    three affine transformations A,B:ℚr→ℚrA,B\colon\mathbb{Q}^{r}\to\mathbb{Q}^{r} and C:ℚ2​r→ℚsC\colon\mathbb{Q}^{2r}\to\mathbb{Q}^{s} with rational valued coefficients (i.e., each is of the form Q​𝒙+𝒃Q\bm{x}+\bm{b} where matrix QQ and vector 𝒃\bm{b} have only rational entries),

  • •

    a mask predicate M:ℕ×ℕ→{⊤,⊥}M\colon\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}\to\{\top,\bot\}, which is defined by M(i,j):=⊤M(i,j):=\top (no masking), M⁡(i,j):=(j<i)M(i,j):=(j<i) (strict future masking), or M⁡(i,j):=(j>i)M(i,j):=(j>i) (strict past masking), and

  • •

    a tie-breaking function τ\tau selecting one element of a finite non-empty subset of ℕ\mathbb{N}, which is either defined as min\min (leftmost tie-breaking) or max\max (rightmost tie-breaking).

We now show how a UHA layer works on a sequence 𝒗1,…,𝒗n∈ℚr\bm{v}_{1},\dots,\bm{v}_{n}\in\mathbb{Q}^{r} with n≥1n\geq 1. The score function is defined as the dot product S⁡(𝒗i,𝒗j):=⟨A⁡(𝒗i),B⁡(𝒗j)⟩S(\bm{v}_{i},\bm{v}_{j}):=\langle A(\bm{v}_{i}),B(\bm{v}_{j})\rangle for all i,j∈[1,n]i,j\in[1,n]. For i∈[1,n]i\in[1,n] let Ui:={j∈[1,n]∣M⁡(i,j)}U_{i}:=\{j\in[1,n]\mid M(i,j)\} be the set of unmasked positions and Bi:={j∈Ui∣∀j′∈Ui:S(𝒗i,𝒗j)≥S(𝒗i,𝒗j′)}B_{i}:=\{j\in U_{i}\mid\forall j^{\prime}\in U_{i}\colon S(\bm{v}_{i},\bm{v}_{j})\geq S(\bm{v}_{i},\bm{v}_{j^{\prime}})\} be the set of unmasked positions that maximize the score function. We define the attention vector at position i∈[1,n]i\in[1,n] as 𝒂i:=𝒗τ⁡(Bi)\bm{a}_{i}:=\bm{v}_{\tau(B_{i})} if Ui≠∅U_{i}\neq\emptyset and 𝒂i:=𝟎\bm{a}_{i}:=\bm{0} otherwise. The layer outputs the sequence C⁡(𝒗1,𝒂1),…,C⁡(𝒗n,𝒂n)C(\bm{v}_{1},\bm{a}_{1}),\dots,C(\bm{v}_{n},\bm{a}_{n}).

ReLU layer.

A ReLU layer of width r>0r>0 on input 𝒗1,…,𝒗n∈ℚr\bm{v}_{1},\dots,\bm{v}_{n}\in\mathbb{Q}^{r} applies for some k∈[1,r]k\in[1,r] the ReLU function to the kk-th coordinate of each 𝒗i\bm{v}_{i}, i.e., it outputs the sequence 𝒗1′,…,𝒗n′\bm{v}^{\prime}_{1},\dots,\bm{v}^{\prime}_{n} where 𝒗i′:=(𝒗i​[1,k−1],max⁡{0,𝒗i​(k)},𝒗i​[k+1,n])\bm{v}^{\prime}_{i}:=(\bm{v}_{i}[1,k-1],\max\{0,\bm{v}_{i}(k)\},\bm{v}_{i}[k+1,n]). [Equivalently, one could instead allow a feed-forward network at the end of an encoder layer (see (Hao et al., 2022; Barceló et al., 2024)).]

Transformer.

A masked unique hard-attention transformer (UHAT) is a length-preserving function 𝒯:Σ∗→(ℚs)∗\mathcal{T}\colon\Sigma^{*}\to(\mathbb{Q}^{s})^{*} defined by application of a token embedding followed by application of a fixed sequence of UHA layers and ReLU layers of matching width.

Languages accepted by UHATs.

To view a UHAT 𝒯:Σ∗→(ℚs)∗\mathcal{T}\colon\Sigma^{*}\to(\mathbb{Q}^{s})^{*} as a language recognizer, we assume that 𝒯\mathcal{T} is given together with an acceptance vector 𝒕∈ℚs\bm{t}\in\mathbb{Q}^{s}. The recognized language L⁡(𝒯)L(\mathcal{T}) is then the set of words on which 𝒯\mathcal{T} outputs a sequence 𝒗1,…,𝒗n∈ℚs\bm{v}_{1},\dots,\bm{v}_{n}\in\mathbb{Q}^{s} with ⟨𝒕,𝒗k⟩>0\langle\bm{t},\bm{v}_{k}\rangle>0, where k∈[1,n]k\in[1,n] is either 1 or nn depending on whether the fist or last position is regarded the output position of 𝒯\mathcal{T}.

2.3 Boolean RASP

As an intermediate step to prove 𝖤𝖷𝖯𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤{\mathsf{EXPSPACE}}-hardness for UHATs, we use Boolean RASP (B-RASP) as introduced by Yang et al. (2024), who showed that B-RASP is expressively equivalent to UHATs. A B-RASP program is defined as follows. Let w=a1​…​an∈Σ∗w=a_{1}\dots a_{n}\in\Sigma^{*} with n≥1n\geq 1 be an input word. For every a∈Σa\in\Sigma there is an initial Boolean vector Qa∈{0,1}nQ_{a}\in\{0,1\}^{n} with Qa​(i)=1Q_{a}(i)=1 iff ai=aa_{i}=a for all i∈[1,n]i\in[1,n]. We number the initial vectors and call them P1,…,P|Σ|P_{1},\dots,P_{|\Sigma|}. We now describe how vector Pt+1P_{t+1} can be defined from vectors P1,…,PtP_{1},\dots,P_{t} for t≥|Σ|t\geq|\Sigma|.

Position-wise operation.

The vector Pt+1P_{t+1} can be defined by Pt+1​(i):=R​(i)P_{t+1}(i):=R(i) for some Boolean combination R⁡(i)R(i) of {P1​(i),…,Pt​(i)}\{P_{1}(i),\dots,P_{t}(i)\}.

Attention operation.

The vector Pt+1P_{t+1} can be defined by either of

Pt+1(i):=◀j[M(i,j),S(i,j)]V(i,j):D(i)\displaystyle P_{t+1}(i):=\ \blacktriangleleft_{j}[M(i,j),S(i,j)]\ V(i,j):D(i)
Pt+1(i):=▶j[M(i,j),S(i,j)]V(i,j):D(i)\displaystyle P_{t+1}(i):=\ \blacktriangleright_{j}[M(i,j),S(i,j)]\ V(i,j):D(i)

where

  • •

    M⁡(i,j)M(i,j) is a mask predicate as in the definition of a UHAT,

  • •

    S⁡(i,j)S(i,j) and V⁡(i,j)V(i,j) are Boolean combinations of {P1​(i),…,Pt​(i)}∪{P1​(j),…,Pt​(j)}\{P_{1}(i),\dots,P_{t}(i)\}\cup\{P_{1}(j),\dots,P_{t}(j)\}, called score predicate and value predicate, respectively,

  • •

    D⁡(i)D(i) is a Boolean combination of {P1​(i),…,Pt​(i)}\{P_{1}(i),\dots,P_{t}(i)\}, called default value predicate.

The semantics of an attention operation is as follows. For every i∈[1,n]i\in[1,n], let

ji:={min⁡{j∈[1,n]∣M⁡(i,j)​ and ​S​(i,j)=1},for ◀max⁡{j∈[1,n]∣M⁡(i,j)​ and ​S​(i,j)=1},for ▶.j_{i}:=\begin{cases}\min\{j\in[1,n]\mid M(i,j)\text{ and }S(i,j)=1\},&\text{for }\blacktriangleleft\\ \max\{j\in[1,n]\mid M(i,j)\text{ and }S(i,j)=1\},&\text{for }\blacktriangleright.\end{cases}

We then define Pt+1​(i):=V⁡(i,ji)P_{t+1}(i):=V(i,j_{i}) if jij_{i} exists and Pt+1​(i):=D​(i)P_{t+1}(i):=D(i) otherwise. Observe that ◀\blacktriangleleft (resp. ▶\blacktriangleright) corresponds to leftmost (resp. rightmost) tie-breaking in UHATs.

A B-RASP program is given by an alphabet Σ\Sigma and a sequence of position-wise and attention operations. We can view a B-RASP program as a language recognizer by designating one Boolean vector YY as the output vector and either the first or last position as the output position. Then an input word w=a1​…​anw=a_{1}\dots a_{n} is accepted if and only if Y⁡(k)=1Y(k)=1, where kk is the output position, i.e., k=1k=1 or k=nk=n.

2.4 Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN)

We use RNN as language acceptors, as in the work of Merrill et al. (2020); Weiss et al. (2024); Weiss et al. (2018). In particular, a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) MM can be viewed as a function g:(ℝd×Σ)→ℝdg:(\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\Sigma)\to\mathbb{R}^{d}. As in the case of transformers, Σ\Sigma is also mapped into ℝk\mathbb{R}^{k} (for some kk) through a token embedding function 𝑒𝑚𝑏\mathit{emb} (e.g. one-hot encoding) and the function gg actually has domain ℝd×ℝk\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{k}. We have an input vector x¯0∈ℝd\bar{x}_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and a final function f:ℝd→{A​c​c,R​e​j}f:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\{Acc,Rej\}, to decide whether a vector x¯∈ℝd\bar{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is accepting. The semantics of acceptance is the same as that of automata, i.e., given w=a1⋯an∈Σ∗w=a_{1}\cdots a_{n}\in\Sigma^{*}, we compute dd-vectors x¯1,…,x¯n\bar{x}_{1},\ldots,\bar{x}_{n} such that g⁡(x¯i,ai+1)=x¯i+1g(\bar{x}_{i},a_{i+1})=\bar{x}_{i+1} for each i=0,…,n−1i=0,\ldots,n-1. The string ww is accepted by MM if f⁡(an)=A​c​cf(a_{n})=Acc.

As a computational model, it is realistic to assume RNNs with a fixed precision, i.e., computation is always done over real numbers that can be represented with a constant kk number of bits. The details of the actual representation are not important for our analysis. Therefore, the state-space QQ of the above RNN can be mapped to dd-vectors over {0,1}k\{0,1\}^{k} (instead of ℝ\mathbb{R}). The following proposition is now immediate.

Proposition 3.

An RNN g:(ℝd×Σ)→ℝdg:(\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\Sigma)\to\mathbb{R}^{d} with fixed precision kk can be represented by a finite automaton with 2k​d2^{kd} many states.

2.5 Size measures and succinctness

Let ℛ\mathcal{R} be a finite representation of a language, i.e., in our case a UHAT, LTL formula, finite automaton, RNN, or B-RASP program. We define the size of ℛ\mathcal{R}, denoted by |ℛ||\mathcal{R}|, as the length of its usual binary encoding. In measuring succinctness of RNN, we put the precision kk in unary also as part of the size measure; since we do not want to compare a transformer that uses a fixed precision kk and allow an RNN that uses a fixed precision 2k2^{k}. Let 𝒞1,𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{1},\mathcal{C}_{2} be classes of finite representations of languages. We say that 𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1} can be exponentially more succinct than 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2} if for every function f∈2o⁡(n)f\in 2^{o(n)} there is an ℛ1∈𝒞1\mathcal{R}_{1}\in\mathcal{C}_{1} such that any ℛ2∈𝒞2\mathcal{R}_{2}\in\mathcal{C}_{2} representing the same language as ℛ1\mathcal{R}_{1} has size |ℛ2|>f⁡(|ℛ1|)|\mathcal{R}_{2}|>f(|\mathcal{R}_{1}|). Similarly, we define doubly exponentially more succinct using functions f∈22o⁡(n)f\in 2^{2^{o(n)}} instead. Intuitively, this means that any translation from 𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1} to 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2} incurs, in the worst-case, an (doubly) exponential increase in size.

3 Size of smallest witness via non-emptiness problem

In this section we consider the problem of checking whether the language recognized by a UHAT or B-RASP program is non-empty. In particular, the technique is essentially a simulation of a Turing machine with an 2O⁡(n)2^{O(n)}-sized tape (for a given nn). As we will see later, there are Turing machines such that the smallest (i.e. shortest) accepted string by the constructed UHAT is of length at least 22Ω⁡(n)2^{2^{\Omega(n)}}.

Example 4.

To illustrate the idea, we describe a B-RASP program that accepts strings of the form

0000​a1​#​0001​a2​#​0010​a3​#​…​#​1111​a24​#0000a_{1}\#0001a_{2}\#0010a_{3}\#\dots\#1111a_{2^{4}}\#

where ai∈{a,b,c}a_{i}\in\{a,b,c\} such that (aj,aj+1)∈H(a_{j},a_{j+1})\in H for all 1≤j<241\leq j<2^{4}. Here, H:={(a,b),(b,c),(b,a),(c,b)}H:=\{(a,b),(b,c),(b,a),(c,b)\} is a set of constraints specifying which symbols can be next to each other. For simplicity, we concentrate on the two main conditions: (i) checking that the bit counter is incremented and (ii) checking that the successive symbols are in HH. To check (i), we use the following attention operation:

C+1(i):=▶j[j<i,Q#(j)]⋁k=14(⋀r=1k−1¬Cr(i)∧Cr(j))∧Ck(i)∧¬Ck(j)∧(⋀r=k+14Cr​(i)↔Cr​(j)):1C_{+1}(i):=\ \blacktriangleright_{j}[j<i,Q_{\#}(j)]\ \bigvee_{k=1}^{4}\big(\bigwedge_{r=1}^{k-1}\neg C_{r}(i)\wedge C_{r}(j)\big)\wedge C_{k}(i)\wedge\neg C_{k}(j)\ \wedge\\ \ \big(\bigwedge_{r=k+1}^{4}C_{r}(i)\leftrightarrow C_{r}(j)\big):1

Assume ii is a #\#-position. Attention selects the rightmost #\#-position jj left of position ii. Let b1i​…​b4ib_{1}^{i}\dots b_{4}^{i} and b1j​…​b4jb_{1}^{j}\dots b_{4}^{j} be the bit strings directly left of position ii and jj, respectively. We assume that we already defined Ck​(i)=bkiC_{k}(i)=b_{k}^{i} and Ck​(j)=bkjC_{k}(j)=b_{k}^{j} for all k∈[1,4]k\in[1,4]. Then the above value predicate checks that the binary number b1i​…​b4ib_{1}^{i}\dots b_{4}^{i} is the number b1j​…​b4jb_{1}^{j}\dots b_{4}^{j} incremented by 1. To check (ii), we can use the attention operation

M←(i):=▶j[j<i,Qa(j)∨Qb(j)∨Qc(j)]⋁(h,h′)∈HQh(j)∧Qh′(i):1.M_{\leftarrow}(i):=\ \blacktriangleright_{j}[j<i,Q_{a}(j)\vee Q_{b}(j)\vee Q_{c}(j)]\ \bigvee_{(h,h^{\prime})\in H}Q_{h}(j)\wedge Q_{h^{\prime}}(i):1.

If ii is a position of a symbol aia_{i}, attention picks the rightmost position jj of a symbol aja_{j} to the left of ii and checks with the value predicate that (aj,ai)∈H(a_{j},a_{i})\in H.

This allows us to succinctly recognize a language whose smallest string has length exponential in the number of bits of the binary counter. By stacking multiple such strings vertically and introducing vertical constraints in addition to the horizontal constraints HH, we can even succinctly recognize languages whose smallest string has doubly exponential length.

We prove the following precise complexity bounds:

Theorem 5.

The non-emptiness problem for UHATs and B-RASP programs is 𝖤𝖷𝖯𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤{\mathsf{EXPSPACE}}-complete.

We start with the lower bound and show it first for B-RASP programs.

Proposition 6.

The non-emptiness problem for B-RASP programs is 𝖤𝖷𝖯𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤{\mathsf{EXPSPACE}}-hard.

For the proof we use the techniques illustrated in Example 4 and reduce from a so-called tiling problem. A tile is a quadruple t∈ℕ04t\in\mathbb{N}_{0}^{4}, where we write t=⟨𝑙𝑒𝑓𝑡⁡(t),𝑢𝑝⁡(t),𝑟𝑖𝑔ℎ𝑡⁡(t),𝑑𝑜𝑤𝑛⁡(t)⟩t=\langle\mathit{left}(t),\mathit{up}(t),\mathit{right}(t),\mathit{down}(t)\rangle. The 2n2^{n}-tiling problem is defined as follows:

Given:

An integer n>0n>0 in unary, a finite set TT of tiles, and a tile t𝑓𝑖𝑛∈Tt_{\mathit{fin}}\in T

Question:

Do there exist m>0m>0 and a function τ:{1,…,2n}×{1,…,m}→T\tau\colon\{1,\dots,2^{n}\}\times\{1,\dots,m\}\to T such that

  1. 1.

    τ⁡(2n,m)=t𝑓𝑖𝑛\tau(2^{n},m)=t_{\mathit{fin}},

  2. 2.

    𝑑𝑜𝑤𝑛⁡(τ⁡(i,1))=𝑢𝑝⁡(τ⁡(i,m))=0\mathit{down}(\tau(i,1))=\mathit{up}(\tau(i,m))=0 for all 1≤i≤2n1\leq i\leq 2^{n},

  3. 3.

    𝑙𝑒𝑓𝑡⁡(τ⁡(1,j))=𝑟𝑖𝑔ℎ𝑡⁡(τ⁡(2n,j))=0\mathit{left}(\tau(1,j))=\mathit{right}(\tau(2^{n},j))=0 for all 1≤j≤m1\leq j\leq m,

  4. 4.

    𝑟𝑖𝑔ℎ𝑡⁡(τ⁡(i,j))=𝑙𝑒𝑓𝑡⁡(τ⁡(i+1,j))\mathit{right}(\tau(i,j))=\mathit{left}(\tau(i+1,j)) for all 1≤i<2n1\leq i<2^{n} and 1≤j≤m1\leq j\leq m, and

  5. 5.

    𝑢𝑝⁡(τ⁡(i,j))=𝑑𝑜𝑤𝑛⁡(τ⁡(i,j+1))\mathit{up}(\tau(i,j))=\mathit{down}(\tau(i,j+1)) for all 1≤i≤2n1\leq i\leq 2^{n} and 1≤j<m1\leq j<m?

The following is shown in (Schwarzentruber, 2019):

Proposition 7.

The 2n2^{n}-tiling problem is 𝖤𝖷𝖯𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤{\mathsf{EXPSPACE}}-complete.

The reduction to B-RASP uses an encoding of the function τ\tau as a sequence of strings which are of a similar form as in Example 4, but is substantially more involved. The key observation is that strict future masking with rightmost tie-breaking enables us to check conditions between successive tiles (condition 4) but also between the current tile and the tile at the most recent past occurrence of the same counter value (condition 5). The full proof can be found in Appendix A.

We observe that the B-RASP program constructed in the proof of Proposition 6 can easily be converted to UHAT, which yields the 𝖤𝖷𝖯𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤{\mathsf{EXPSPACE}} lower bound also for UHAT.

Proposition 8.

The non-emptiness problem for UHAT is 𝖤𝖷𝖯𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤{\mathsf{EXPSPACE}}-hard.

Proof sketch.

We show that the B-RASP program constructed in the proof of Proposition 6 can be converted to a UHAT in polynomial time. To this end, note that Boolean operations can easily be simulated using affine transformations and ReLU. For the attention operations we use an attention layer. The value predicates V⁡(i,j)V(i,j) can be simulated by copying the required components of the jj-th vector, that was selected by attention, to the ii-th vector using the affine transformation whose result is forwarded and computing the result of the Boolean combination with additional ReLU layers. For the score predicates S⁡(i,j)S(i,j) we note that they either only depend on jj or they check whether some binary numbers at positions ii and jj are equal. The former can be simulated using an additional preliminary layer that already computes the result of S⁡(j)S(j) for every position jj. For the latter we use Lemma 9. ∎

The proof of the following Lemma can be found in Appendix A.

Lemma 9.

Given a mask predicate MM and tie-breaking function τ\tau, there is an attention layer using MM and τ\tau that on every sequence 𝐯1,…,𝐯n∈{0,1}2​d\bm{v}_{1},\dots,\bm{v}_{n}\in\{0,1\}^{2d} with 𝐯k=(bk,1,1−bk,1,…,bk,d,1−bk,d)\bm{v}_{k}=(b_{k,1},1-b_{k,1},\dots,b_{k,d},1-b_{k,d}) for all k∈[1,n]k\in[1,n] and for every i∈[1,n]i\in[1,n] picks attention vector 𝐚i=𝐯j\bm{a}_{i}=\bm{v}_{j} such that bi,r=bj,rb_{i,r}=b_{j,r} for all r∈[1,d]r\in[1,d] if such an unmasked position jj exists.

We observe that the B-RASP program constructed in the proof of Proposition 6 only uses strict future masking and rightmost tie-breaking. Thus, the 𝖤𝖷𝖯𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤{\mathsf{EXPSPACE}} lower bound already holds for UHATs that only use strict future masking and rightmost tie-breaking (similar for strict past masking and leftmost tie-breaking).

Corollary 10.

The non-emptiness problem for UHATs, where every layer uses strict future masking and rightmost tie-breaking (resp. strict past masking and leftmost tie-breaking), is already 𝖤𝖷𝖯𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤{\mathsf{EXPSPACE}}-hard.

We now prove the upper bounds in Theorem 5. To this end, we first note that any B-RASP program can be converted in exponential time into an LTL formula using the construction from (Yang et al., 2024). In Proposition 12 we prove that the same is true for UHATs, which improves the doubly exponential construction in (Yang et al., 2024) that translates UHATs to B-RASP programs first. This suffices to prove the exponential-space upper bounds in Theorem 5 since non-emptiness of languages given by LTL formulas can be checked in polynomial space (Sistla & Clarke, 1985).

For the translation from UHAT to LTL, we first have to make the crucial observation that the values occurring during the computation of a UHAT are not “too large”.

Proposition 11.

The values occurring in the computation of a UHAT 𝒯\mathcal{T} can be represented with only a polynomial number of bits in the size of 𝒯\mathcal{T}. Thus, rational numbers with fixed precision, that is polynomial in the size of 𝒯\mathcal{T}, are sufficient.

Proof.

Clearly, ReLU layers do not increase the amount of bits needed since only the maximum with 0 is taken. Since our UHAT model is defined over rational numbers, we can represent each value with a binary number for the numerator and a binary number for the denominator. By taking the LCM, we can further assume that the denominators of the numbers in 𝑒𝑚𝑏⁡(Σ)\mathit{emb}(\Sigma) are all equal. Note that the LCM of linearly many numbers of linear bit size can be represented with polynomially many bits. Similarly, for each attention layer we can assume that the denominators of all coefficients of the affine transformation, whose result is forwarded, are equal. This ensure that in the input sequence and after each layer the values have the same denominator. Next we argue that the numerators and denominators of all values that occur in the computation can be represented with a polynomial number of bits. The output of an attention layer is an affine transformation involving two input vectors. Here, the input values are only multiplied with constants, i.e., the values in the output only depend linearly on input values. Since the denominators of the values after multiplication with coefficients are all equal, addition does not incur an increase in bit length of the denominators. Therefore, a repeated application of linearly many attention layers can only lead to numerators and denominators whose values are at most exponential in the number of layers, i.e., can be represented with polynomially many bits. For the score function we observe that the dot product after an affine transformation only involves two input vectors. Thus, the number of bits needed to represent the result of the score function is still polynomial. A crucial observation is that the results after applying the score function are not forwarded to the next layer, which would introduce an exponential increase in size in the number of layers. ∎

By Proposition 11, we can already compute the results of the affine transformations and score functions during the construction of the LTL formula. This means that the LTL formula only has to simulate the position-wise behavior of attention layers, i.e., masking and selecting the position of the attention vector, but not the actual computation of values. The proof of the following proposition can be found in Appendix A.

Proposition 12.

Given a UHAT that recognizes a language LL, one can construct in exponential time an LTL formula recognizing LL.

We remark that if we start with a UHAT, where every attention layer uses strict future masking and leftmost tie-breaking (resp. strict past masking and rightmost tie-breaking), then the LTL formula constructed in the proof of Proposition 12 only uses the P (resp. F) operator. It was shown in (Sistla & Clarke, 1985) that the non-emptiness problem for the fragments of LTL that only allow P or F is 𝖭𝖯{\mathsf{NP}}-complete. Thus, we obtain an improved complexity upper bound for such restricted UHATs.

Corollary 13.

The non-emptiness problem for UHATs, where every attention layer uses strict future masking and leftmost tie-breaking (resp. strict past masking and rightmost tie-breaking), is in 𝖭𝖤𝖷𝖯{\mathsf{NEXP}}.

Note that it was already shown in (Jerad et al., 2025) that such restricted UHATs are equally expressive as the LTL fragment with only P (resp. F). However, the construction by Jerad et al. (2025) from UHAT to the LTL fragments incurs a doubly exponential blow-up, as opposed to our singly exponential translation.

4 Succinctness against other representations of languages

We now study how succinctly transformers can represent languages compared to standard models from formal language theory.

We first compare transformers to LTL. One indication that transformers may be more succinct than LTL comes from Theorem 5, which shows that the non-emptiness problem for UHATs is 𝖤𝖷𝖯𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤{\mathsf{EXPSPACE}}-complete, whereas for LTL the corresponding problem is known to be 𝖯𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤{\mathsf{PSPACE}}-complete. The following result shows that this exponential gap also manifests in terms of succinctness.

Theorem 14.

UHATs can be exponentially more succinct than LTL.

Proof.

We give a family {Ln}n≥1\{L_{n}\}_{n\geq 1} of languages such that LnL_{n} is recognized by a UHAT of size polynomial in nn but any LTL formula recognizing LnL_{n} has size exponential in nn. Let ℳn\mathcal{M}_{n} be a (deterministic) Turing machine that implements a binary counter with 2n2^{n} bits, i.e., when initialized with 02n0^{2^{n}}, it increments the binary number until it has written 12n1^{2^{n}} on its tape and accepts. Clearly, ℳn\mathcal{M}_{n} is of size polynomial in nn, it uses an exponential number of tape cells in nn, and the unique accepting run has length at least 22n2^{2^{n}}. In (van Emde Boas, 1997) a reduction from Turing machines to tiling problem instances is presented that encodes configurations of Turing machines in its rows and a correct tiling corresponds to a valid execution of the Turing machine. We observe that the 2n2^{n}-tiling problem instance ℐn\mathcal{I}_{n} constructed from ℳn\mathcal{M}_{n} has size polynomial in nn and it has the property that the smallest correct tiling has at least 22n2^{2^{n}} many rows. In the proof of Proposition 8 we showed that there is a UHAT 𝒯n\mathcal{T}_{n} of size polynomial in the size of ℐn\mathcal{I}_{n} that recognizes encodings of correct tilings of ℐn\mathcal{I}_{n}. Thus, 𝒯n\mathcal{T}_{n} is of size polynomial in nn and the smallest accepted word has length at least 22n2^{2^{n}}. We let LnL_{n} be the language recognized by 𝒯n\mathcal{T}_{n}. Let φn\varphi_{n} be an LTL formula that recognizes LnL_{n}. Since the smallest accepted word by any LTL formula has length at most exponential in the formula size (using an exponential conversion from LTL to finite automata similar to (Vardi & Wolper, 1994)), it follows that the size of φn\varphi_{n} is at least exponential in nn. ∎

Conversely, we can show that there is no language than can be represented by LTL significantly more succinct than by UHATs. Thus, we may even say that UHATs are exponentially more succinct than LTL.

Proposition 15.

Given an LTL formula φ\varphi, one can construct in polynomial time a UHAT that recognizes the same language as φ\varphi.

Proof sketch.

From φ\varphi we construct a UHAT 𝒯\mathcal{T} that on input ww outputs in a dedicated component at position 1≤i≤|w|1\leq i\leq|w| a 1 if w,i⊧φw,i\models\varphi and a 0 otherwise. Then the claim can be proven by induction. If φ\varphi is an atomic formula or a Boolean combination, we can easily define 𝒯\mathcal{T}. If φ=φ1Sφ2\varphi=\varphi_{1}\mathbin{\textbf{S}}\varphi_{2}, we can assume by induction hypothesis that we already computed the truth value of φ1\varphi_{1} and φ2\varphi_{2} at every position, which we use to compute the truth value of ¬φ1∨φ2\neg\varphi_{1}\vee\varphi_{2}. We then use an attention layer with strict future masking and rightmost tie-breaking to get for every position ii the maximal position j<ij<i where ¬φ1∨φ2\neg\varphi_{1}\vee\varphi_{2} holds and output at position ii the truth value of φ2\varphi_{2} from position jj. The case where φ=φ1Uφ2\varphi=\varphi_{1}\mathbin{\textbf{U}}\varphi_{2} is similar using strict past masking and leftmost tie-breaking. ∎

We show next that compared to finite automata, UHATs can be even doubly exponentially more succinct. To see this, take the UHAT 𝒯n\mathcal{T}_{n} from the proof of Theorem 14 that is of size polynomial in nn and the smallest accepted word has length at least 22n2^{2^{n}}. Since any automaton recognizing a non-empty language accepts a word of length at most linear in the automaton size, the smallest automaton that recognizes the same language as 𝒯n\mathcal{T}_{n} has size at least doubly exponential in nn.

Theorem 16.

UHATs can be doubly exponentially more succinct than finite automata.

Conversely, the best known construction from counter-free automata (that are equally expressive as LTL) to LTL incurs an exponential blow-up (Maler & Pnueli, 1990). Thus, together with Proposition 15, we obtain an exponential-time translation from counter-free automata to UHATs. Note that also the translation in (Yang et al., 2024) from counter-free automata to UHATs increases the size exponentially, when using the results by Maler & Pnueli (1990).

Finally, we combine Theorem 16 and Proposition 3 to obtain the following succinctness gap between UHATs and RNNs.

Corollary 17.

UHATs can be exponentially more succinct than RNNs.

5 Applications

As a consequence of our results, we can show that reasoning about languages of UHATs (e.g. equivalence, emptiness, universality, etc.) is provably intractable. Contrast this to deterministic finite automata, where all these problems can be done in polynomial time (cf. (Kozen, 1997)). In the following, we show the precise complexity for the equivalence problem, i.e., the problem of checking whether two given UHATs recognize the same language. That the universality problem is 𝖤𝖷𝖯𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤{\mathsf{EXPSPACE}}-complete can be proven similarly.

Theorem 18.

Equivalence of UHATs is 𝖤𝖷𝖯𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤{\mathsf{EXPSPACE}}-complete.

Proof.

To prove the lower bound, we reduce from the non-emptiness problem for UHATs, which by Theorem 5 is 𝖤𝖷𝖯𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤{\mathsf{EXPSPACE}}-complete. To this end, let 𝒯\mathcal{T} be a given UHAT and fix a UHAT 𝒯0\mathcal{T}_{0} that recognizes the empty language. Then we have that 𝒯\mathcal{T} and 𝒯0\mathcal{T}_{0} are equivalent if and only if 𝒯\mathcal{T} recognizes the empty language.

For the upper bound let the UHATs 𝒯1\mathcal{T}_{1} and 𝒯2\mathcal{T}_{2} be given. We apply Proposition 12 to turn 𝒯1\mathcal{T}_{1} and 𝒯2\mathcal{T}_{2} in exponential time into LTL formulas φ1\varphi_{1} and φ2\varphi_{2}, respectively. Now, 𝒯1\mathcal{T}_{1} and 𝒯2\mathcal{T}_{2} are equivalent if and only if φ1\varphi_{1} and φ2\varphi_{2} are equivalent. The latter can be decided in polynomial space (Sistla & Clarke, 1985), which results in an exponential-space algorithm in total. ∎

6 Concluding remarks

Related work.

Our work was inspired by the works of Yang et al. (2024); Barceló et al. (2024); Jerad et al. (2025); Li & Cotterell (2025), which exhibit a close connection between unique-hard attention transformers and star-free regular languages. In particular, these works also exploited the connection to LTL. However, none of these results investigated neither the issue of succinctness nor computational complexity of verification, which we establish in this paper.

Sälzer et al. (2025) investigated the issue of verifying transformers of various precisions. In particular, it was shown that transformers of fixed precision are at least 𝖭𝖤𝖷𝖯{\mathsf{NEXP}}-hard (i.e. hard for the class of problems solvable by nondeterministic algorithms that run in exponential time). The technique there implies that transformers are (singly) exponentially more succinct than finite automata. However, no conclusion can be derived as to their succinctness relative to representations like LTL or RNN. Our result substantially improve this by showing that transformers are doubly exponentially more succinct than automata, and exponentially more succinct than LTL and RNN. In addition, our work assumes a much simpler model in comparison to the results in (Sälzer et al., 2025). In particular, we use unique-hard attention, whereas in (Sälzer et al., 2025) a combination of softmax and hardmax is employed. Finally, our results use positional masking (as employed in (Yang et al., 2024; Jerad et al., 2025; Li & Cotterell, 2025)) — as a simple class of Positional Embeddings (PEs) — in contrast to (Sälzer et al., 2025), which admits arbitrary PEs of fixed precision.

Succinctness has also been studied in the context of linguistics. For example, according to Zipf’s law of abbreviation (Zipf, 1935), frequently occuring concepts tend to have a succinct description. In particular, Hindu-Arabic numeral system — which evolves into our modern numeral system — allows an exponentially more succinct description than the Roman numeral system. According to Zipf’s law, the former potentially enables mathematics and computer science as we see today.

Future work.

We mention the challenge of developing an automatic tool for analyzing, verifying, and explaining transformers. More broadly, this is an important problem for explainable AI, as thoroughly described in the survey (Huang et al., 2020). In particular, lots of practical advances have been made on verifying feed-forward neural networks (but not transformers) and some practical tools have been developed in the last decade (see also the results of the most recent annual VNN competition (Brix et al., 2024)). Despite the rather high complexity (𝖤𝖷𝖯𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤{\mathsf{EXPSPACE}}-complete), we pose as a challenge to exploit techniques from automated verification (Clarke et al., 2018) (e.g. symbolic techniques, simulation, etc.) to verify transformers in practice.

𝑒𝑛𝑐τ​(i,j):=⟨i−1⟩​τ​(i,j)​#\mathit{enc}_{\tau}(i,j):=\langle i-1\rangle\tau(i,j)\#

𝑒𝑛𝑐⁡(τ):=𝑒𝑛𝑐τ​(1,1)​…​𝑒𝑛𝑐τ​(2n,1)​𝑒𝑛𝑐τ​(2,1)​…​𝑒𝑛𝑐τ​(m,2n).\mathit{enc}(\tau):=\mathit{enc}_{\tau}(1,1)\dots\mathit{enc}_{\tau}(2^{n},1)\mathit{enc}_{\tau}(2,1)\dots\mathit{enc}_{\tau}(m,2^{n}).

A.2 Proof of Lemma 9

As affine transformations AA and BB we use the identity, i.e.,

S⁡(𝒗i,𝒗j):=⟨𝒗i,𝒗j⟩=∑r=1d(bi,r​bj,r+(1−bi,r)​(1−bj,r))S(\bm{v}_{i},\bm{v}_{j}):=\langle\bm{v}_{i},\bm{v}_{j}\rangle=\sum_{r=1}^{d}\big(b_{i,r}b_{j,r}+(1-b_{i,r})(1-b_{j,r})\big)

which is equal to |{r∈[1,d]∣bi,r=bj,r}||\{r\in[1,d]\mid b_{i,r}=b_{j,r}\}| since

bi,r​bj,r+(1−bi,r)​(1−bj,r)={1,if ​bi,r=bj,r0,otherwise.b_{i,r}b_{j,r}+(1-b_{i,r})(1-b_{j,r})=\begin{cases}1,&\text{if }b_{i,r}=b_{j,r}\\ 0,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}

Thus, the score is maximized (equal to dd) if bi,r=bj,rb_{i,r}=b_{j,r} for all r∈[1,d]r\in[1,d].

A.3 Proof of Proposition 12

Let 𝒯\mathcal{T} be a UHAT that recognizes a language L⊆Σ∗L\subseteq\Sigma^{*} and FF be a set of binary representations of rational numbers that may occur during the computation of 𝒯\mathcal{T} from Proposition 11. Our goal is to define for the ℓ\ell-th layer of 𝒯\mathcal{T} and every vector 𝒗∈Fs\bm{v}\in F^{s}, where ss is the output dimension of layer ℓ\ell, an LTL formula φ𝒗ℓ\varphi_{\bm{v}}^{\ell} such that if 𝒯\mathcal{T} is applied on input w∈Σw\in\Sigma, then the ℓ\ell-th layer outputs at position i∈[1,|w|]i\in[1,|w|] the vector 𝒗\bm{v} if and only if w,i⊧φ𝒗ℓw,i\models\varphi_{\bm{v}}^{\ell}. We define this formula inductively on the layer number ℓ\ell. Let 𝑒𝑚𝑏:Σ→(ℚd)∗\mathit{emb}\colon\Sigma\to(\mathbb{Q}^{d})^{*} be the token embedding of 𝒯\mathcal{T}. For all 𝒗∈Fd\bm{v}\in F^{d} let

φ𝒗0:={⋁a∈𝑒𝑚𝑏−1​(𝒗)Qa,if ​𝑒𝑚𝑏−1​(𝒗)≠∅⊥,otherwise.\varphi_{\bm{v}}^{0}:=\begin{cases}\bigvee_{a\in\mathit{emb}^{-1}(\bm{v})}Q_{a},&\text{if }\mathit{emb}^{-1}(\bm{v})\neq\emptyset\\ \bot,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}

We now define the formula for layer ℓ+1\ell+1. In case of a ReLU layer of width rr, that applies ReLU to the kk-th coordinate, we can simply define

φ𝒗ℓ+1:=⋁u∈F:max⁡{0,u}=𝒗⁡[k]φ(𝒗⁡[1,k−1],u,𝒗⁡[k+1,r])ℓ\varphi_{\bm{v}}^{\ell+1}:=\bigvee_{u\in F\colon\max\{0,u\}=\bm{v}[k]}\varphi_{(\bm{v}[1,k-1],u,\bm{v}[k+1,r])}^{\ell}

We omit this special case in the following. If the layer uses leftmost tie-breaking, we adapt the formula as follows:

If the layer uses no masking and rightmost tie-breaking, we distinguish three situations: the attention vector is at the current position, the attention vector is strictly to the left of the current position, or the attention vector is strictly to the right of the current position. Thus, in the case of no masking and rightmost tie-breaking, we define φ𝒗ℓ+1\varphi_{\bm{v}}^{\ell+1} as the disjunction of Eqs. 1, 2 and 3. The case where the layer uses no masking and leftmost tie-breaking is analogous.

Finally, if there are mm layers, where the last layer outputs vectors of dimension ss, and 𝒕∈ℚs\bm{t}\in\mathbb{Q}^{s} is the acceptance vector of 𝒯\mathcal{T}, we define the formula

φ:=⋁𝒗∈Fs:⟨𝒕,𝒗⟩>0φ𝒗m.\varphi:=\bigvee_{\bm{v}\in F^{s}\colon\\ \langle\bm{t},\bm{v}\rangle>0}\varphi_{\bm{v}}^{m}.

Then w,k⊧φw,k\models\varphi if and only if w∈Lw\in L, where kk is the output position of 𝒯\mathcal{T}.

It remains to argue that φ\varphi can be computed in exponential time. By Proposition 11, |F||F| is exponential in the size of 𝒯\mathcal{T} and every representation in FF is of polynomial size. Moreover, FF can be computed in exponential time. The formulas φ𝒗ℓ+1\varphi_{\bm{v}}^{\ell+1} at every layer ℓ+1\ell+1 of width rr depends on |F|O⁡(r)|F|^{O(r)} many formulas from layer ℓ\ell. Moreover, φ𝒗ℓ+1\varphi_{\bm{v}}^{\ell+1} can be computed in time polynomial in |F|r⋅|𝒯||F|^{r}\cdot|\mathcal{T}|, since we only have to compute affine transformations on vectors from FrF^{r}, where each component is of size polynomial in |𝒯||\mathcal{T}|. The formulas φ𝒗m\varphi_{\bm{v}}^{m} at the last layer mm depend on |F|O⁡(r′​m)|F|^{O(r^{\prime}m)} many formulas from layer 0, where r′r^{\prime} is the maximum width of all layers. Thus, φ𝒗m\varphi_{\bm{v}}^{m} has size exponential in |𝒯||\mathcal{T}| and can be computed in exponential time. Therefore, also φ\varphi can be computed in exponential time.
